name: Brooklyn Banks
why: The wave-like brick banks under the Manhattan side of the Brooklyn Bridge were a cornerstone of New York street skating until they closed for bridge work in 2010; the big banks reopened to the public on June 5, 2025, with skate space developed alongside Gotham Park and The Skatepark Project.
heads_up: The city has budgeted a further rebuild of the space under the bridge (The Arches), so check for construction fencing before you make the trip.

name: Lower East Side Skatepark (Coleman Playground)
why: Concrete park under the Manhattan Bridge, rebuilt in 2012 to a design donated by Steve Rodriguez and built by California Skateparks; its central location makes it a regular stop for jams, demos and best-trick contests.
heads_up: NYC Parks requires a helmet plus knee and elbow pads here; open dawn to dusk, and the bridge overhead keeps parts of it dry in light rain.

name: Pier 62 Skatepark
why: Opened in May 2010 on a Hudson River Park pier in Chelsea, this 15,000 sq ft concrete park by California Skateparks and Site Design Group has a 10-foot pool that runs to vert, a flow area with a clamshell and a small street section.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to dusk; the deep end of the pool is 10 ft, so know your transition before you drop in.

name: Golconda Skate Park (Fat Kid Spot)
why: Started as the DIY 'Fat Kid Spot' under the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway near DUMBO and reopened in 2016 as an 18,000 sq ft concrete and brick park designed with advice from Steve Rodriguez.
heads_up: Locals and the NYC Skateboard Coalition keep a tool box on site and hold monthly clean-ups, so grab a broom if the surface is dusty; the expressway overhead gives some cover.

name: Millennium Skate Park (Owl's Head)
why: Brooklyn's first concrete skatepark, opened in 2001 in Owl's Head Park in Bay Ridge and designed by Andy Kessler; about 14,000 sq ft with a street section and bowls up to 8 ft deep.
heads_up: Helmet rule is enforced; the NYC Skateboard Coalition holds a yearly pool-series event here, which fills the bowl.

name: Andy Kessler Skatepark
why: Manhattan's first full-size public skatepark, built in 1995–96 by Andy Kessler with local teens in Riverside Park; rebuilt in concrete by California Skateparks in 2019 with a street plaza, a 4-ft mini ramp and an 11-ft pool with pool coping.
heads_up: In Riverside Park at 108th Street; the pool's deep end has 18 inches of vert.

name: Tompkins Square Park
why: A paved corner of this East Village park has been a daily flatground and meeting spot for New York skaters for decades; in 2019 NYC Parks dropped a plan to turf it after a petition gathered more than 32,000 signatures.
heads_up: It's a shared public park, not a built skatepark — mostly flat ground, so give other park users room.

name: Rockaway Beach Skatepark
why: Beachside park by the Rockaway boardwalk at Beach 91st Street; the worn wooden original, battered by a hurricane, was replaced with a concrete park with a triple-set hubba, ledges and a transition section off to the side.
heads_up: Little standing room except the edges, and scooter riders favour the kicker-ledge bank — expect to share lines.

name: Mullaly Skate Park
why: Installed in 1988 in Mullaly Park on 164th Street near Yankee Stadium, it is one of New York City's first public skateparks.
heads_up: Sits between Jerome and River Avenues by Yankee Stadium; check NYC Parks for current hours and rules.

name: Montauk Skate Park
why: A 20,000 sq ft concrete park opened in 2022 by American Ramp Company and Pivot Customs, with a flow bowl, a snake run, a bowl with pool coping and a full street section at the tip of Long Island.
heads_up: Outdoor concrete at the far end of Long Island — check the forecast before making the drive.

name: ROC City Skatepark
why: Built under the Frederick Douglass–Susan B. Anthony Bridge after a nearly 20-year effort by local skaters and the city; Phase 1, focused on transition, opened in fall 2020, and a 13,000 sq ft street plaza (Phase 2) was set to follow.
heads_up: Phase 2 construction next door was scheduled to finish in fall 2026 — expect fencing on the south side until it opens.

name: Alix Rice Peace Park Skatepark
why: Grindline-built park just outside Buffalo with a flow bowl (waterfall, extension and radial pocket), a separate pool and a street section with stairs, a hubba, a handrail and a round manual pad.
heads_up: Outdoor concrete — the pool and flow bowl need time to dry out after rain.

name: Seven Presidents Skatepark
why: Oceanfront Spohn Ranch park of about 21,000 sq ft in Seven Presidents Oceanfront Park, rebuilt after Hurricane Sandy and later expanded with a second flow bowl.
heads_up: Beachfront park — summer beach traffic and parking can be tight; check hours and any fee before you go.

name: Berry Lane Skatepark
why: A 12,000 sq ft park that reopened in 2020 as part of the Berry Lane Park rebuild, pairing a street course (flat bars, stair sets, a camel hump) with a flow bowl.
heads_up: Part of a larger rebuilt city park; check Jersey City recreation for current hours.

name: Ocean City Skatepark
why: A 12,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch park in the Jersey Shore resort town, with a flow bowl, a snake run, hubba ledges, a four-stair and a mini ramp.
heads_up: Shore town in summer — check the city for hours and any pass or fee before you go.

name: Toms River Skatepark
why: A 7,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch park built in 2021, with a bowl that runs from a 4-ft shallow end to a 6-ft deep end, a half pyramid, a hubba ledge and a euro gap.
heads_up: Listed as open 24/7, but it's unstaffed — skate with a friend after dark.

name: FDR Skatepark
why: Skater-built concrete under I-95 in South Philadelphia's FDR Park, grown since the mid-1990s with volunteer labour and donated materials; it hosted the 2005 Gravity Games and still runs on upkeep paid for by the people who skate it.
heads_up: Steep, homemade transitions — watch a few runs before you jump in; the highway overhead keeps much of it dry, and donations to the upkeep crew are welcome.

name: Paine's Park
why: About 30,000 sq ft of skate plaza on the Schuylkill River banks below the Philadelphia Museum of Art, conceived by the Franklin's Paine Skatepark Fund in 2002 and opened in 2013.
heads_up: Shared public space next to the river trail, with food trucks and events at times — keep an eye out for walkers.

name: Pitcher Park Memorial Skate Park
why: Grindline-built park of about 17,000 sq ft in Carnegie Park, the largest concrete skatepark in the Pittsburgh area, with a 20-ft-diameter full pipe between two bowls and a flowing street section.
heads_up: Directly off the Parkway West and I-79 and reachable by public transit from Pittsburgh.

name: Woodward Pennsylvania (Open Ride Sessions)
why: The original Woodward action-sports camp, running in central Pennsylvania for about 50 years; outside summer camp it sells public open-ride days on select weekends, with the indoor parks open on the late-autumn dates.
heads_up: Not drop-in: buy open-ride access online in advance; certified helmets are required and minors must be with an adult.

name: Bethlehem SkatePlaza
why: A 23,000 sq ft street plaza on the South Bethlehem Greenway that stretches more than 750 ft and recreates city obstacles — handrails, benches, staircases and sculptures.
heads_up: Open dawn to dusk every day, weather permitting; it's across from the Wind Creek casino on Steel Avenue.

name: Lynch Family Skatepark
why: About 40,000 sq ft beneath the Zakim Bridge ramps, opened in 2015 after a long Charles River Conservancy campaign; Stantec designed it and California Skateparks built it, with three bowls up to about 11.5 ft deep and a street plaza.
heads_up: Partly covered by the highway, so some lines stay dry in light rain; BMX, inline and scooters are allowed too, so share the bowls.

name: Oak Crest Cove Skatepark
why: Cape Cod concrete park opened in 2020 with a flow bowl, a 6–9 ft amoeba bowl with extensions and hips, and a street area with ledges, manual pads and rails.
heads_up: The amoeba bowl reaches 9 ft at its deepest — know your transition.

name: North Adams Skatepark (Unity Skate Park)
why: An 11,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch street park built in 2017 in the Berkshires, with down, out and flat ledges, handrails, stairs, a pole jam and a euro gap.
heads_up: Mostly street terrain — bring your ledge game rather than your bowl board.

name: Rockwell Skatepark
why: An 18,000 sq ft concrete park in Rockwell Park designed by Site Design Group and built by California Skateparks, with a bowl that runs from a shallow to a deep end, stairs, hubbas and a bench-over-gap.
heads_up: Unsupervised city park — the deep end of the bowl is for confident riders.

name: Scalzi Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft Grindline park built in 2007 in Scalzi Park, with transitions, hips, transfers, an over-vert section and pool coping alongside a small street area.
heads_up: Tight, transition-heavy layout — the over-vert section is for experienced riders.

name: Old Mountain Field Skatepark
why: Open since 2000 and added to over the years, this Peace Dale park mixes a long street course (rails, flat bars, pole jams, ledges, stairs) with a pool-style bowl that has a shallow and a deep end.
heads_up: Inside the Old Mountain Field sports complex on Kingstown Road in Peace Dale.

name: Jamestown Skatepark
why: Island park on Conanicut Island built in the early 2000s, with a double bowl joined by a spine, pool and steel coping, hips and pockets, plus a pyramid and a vert wall.
heads_up: Jamestown is reached by bridge from Newport or North Kingstown; the bowls are the draw.

name: Andy "A_Dog" Williams Skatepark
why: A 21,000 sq ft waterfront park on Lake Champlain designed by Grindline and built by Artisan Skateparks in 2015, with a large central flow bowl, a mini bowl, a big vert bank and street lines.
heads_up: On the Burlington waterfront beside Lake Champlain — walkers and cyclists pass right by.

name: Talent Skatepark
why: Vermont's long-running indoor skatepark and shop, open since 2001 and reopened as a nonprofit in January 2020 after closing in 2018; sessions run in two-hour blocks year-round.
heads_up: Reserve a session online and sign a waiver first; helmets and sneakers required (rental helmets $5), and Saturday 10–12 is beginners only.

name: David W. Deane Skateboard Park
why: A 20,000 sq ft Pillar Design and Artisan Skateparks build with two pool-style bowls, extensions, hips, volcanoes and a keyhole, plus ledges and a kicker with a fire hydrant.
heads_up: Transition-heavy park — the pool-style bowls are the main event.

name: Chris Rice Skateboard Park
why: Portsmouth's skatepark on Greenland Road, opened December 21, 2023, next to the Seacoast Greenway and the city bike park; volunteers added a pump track beside it in 2024.
heads_up: Lit in the evening: the lights dim 30 and 15 minutes before closing and switch off at close; no e-bikes, e-scooters or electric boards on the surface.

name: Red Alert Skatepark
why: Indoor park and skate shop in downtown Rochester with quarter pipes, banks, rails, ledges, a pyramid, a euro gap and a mini ramp — one of the few places to skate indoors in New Hampshire.
heads_up: Paid sessions — check the shop's current hours and rates before driving in.

name: Dougherty Field Skatepark
why: Portland's city skatepark at Dougherty Field, recently expanded with new concrete areas designed with Pillar Design and built with Artisan Skateparks.
heads_up: Fresh concrete and grass were still settling after the expansion — stay off fenced or seeded areas.

name: Skatepark of Baltimore
why: An 11,000 sq ft concrete park in Roosevelt Park in Hampden, opened in 2016, with deep bowls, stairs, ledges and a small handrail.
heads_up: Daytime hours only; the deep bowls are not for first-timers.

name: Ocean Bowl Skatepark
why: Opened in June 1976 as the first skatepark on the East Coast and described as the longest-running municipal skatepark in the US; it was rebuilt on the same site in 1998 and has hosted the Dew Tour.
heads_up: Resort-town park — check the town's hours and admission before you go.

name: Olney Manor Skatepark
why: A 14,400 sq ft Montgomery County park designed by Site Design Group and built by California Skateparks, with a 10-ft bowl with pool coping and a street section.
heads_up: Open daytime hours; the 10-ft bowl is the deep end — mind it.

name: Hagerstown Skatepark
why: A Spohn Ranch park opened in 2022 with a mini ramp, a flow bowl, ledges and a skateable 'H' sculpture, plus a pump track.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset.

name: Greenbelt Skatepark
why: A 7,000 sq ft California Skateparks build with a 10.5-ft peanut bowl with pool coping, a kidney bowl, banks, hips and ledges.
heads_up: Bowl-first park — the peanut bowl's deep end is 10.5 ft.

name: Freedom Plaza
why: Open plaza at 14th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW whose open hardscape and railings have long drawn skaters from across the country.
heads_up: Skating is not permitted — the plaza is National Park Service land and Park Police regularly move skaters on; respect the inlaid L'Enfant plan.

name: Mount Trashmore Skatepark
why: A 24,000 sq ft park in Mount Trashmore Park, opened in 2003 and rebuilt in 2007 after a fire, with a big street course, a 7-ft above-ground bowl and a competition vert ramp over 13 ft tall and 40 ft wide; Tony Hawk is among the pros who have skated it.
heads_up: Check the city's hours and any helmet or pass rules before you go.

name: Powhatan Springs Skatepark
why: A 17,000 sq ft Team Pain park in Arlington with an 11-ft kidney bowl, a 5-ft bowl, a snake run and a street section with handrails and a euro gap.
heads_up: The 11-ft kidney bowl is for confident bowl riders.

name: Texas Beach Skatepark
why: A DIY park built by local skaters and volunteers in the Texas Beach riverside area on the James River, reached from the North Bank Trail.
heads_up: DIY spot with no staff — skate at your own risk, and help keep it clean.

name: Charlottesville Skatepark
why: Charlottesville's city park, split into a transition side with several bowls and a separate street side with ledges, rails and stairs.
heads_up: Two parks in one — warm up on the street side before the bowls.

name: Warren County Skatepark
why: A 17,000 sq ft Pillar Design and Artisan Skateparks build in the Shenandoah Valley, with a pool-style bowl, a flow bowl with hips and a spine, and a street section with a vert quarter pipe.
heads_up: Front Royal sits at the north end of Skyline Drive, just off I-66.

name: Lake Fairfax Skatepark
why: A 16,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch park opened in 2012 in Lake Fairfax Park, with a clover-shaped bowl with hips and a pocket and a street section with hubbas, handrails, stairs and a pole jam.
heads_up: Inside a Fairfax County park — check the county for hours and any entry rules before you go.

name: Wheeling Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft Grindline park built in 2007, with a 4–10 ft bowl with an island, hips and extensions, and a street section with stairs and rails.
heads_up: Listed as open 24/7, but there's no staff — skate with a friend after dark.

name: Fort Neal Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft Grindline park with a 6–10 ft clover bowl with pool coping and a full street section with stairs, handrails and a euro gap.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset.

name: Fayetteville Town Park Skatepark
why: A Grindline park in the New River Gorge town of Fayetteville, with a kidney bowl with stairs and pool coping, a flow bowl and a street section.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset; easy to pair with a trip to the New River Gorge.

name: Skatepark of Charleston
why: Downtown Charleston park under Interstate 64 with a mini ramp, quarter pipes, a spine, a pyramid, ledges and rails.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.; the interstate overhead keeps it partly sheltered from rain.
